title: Yield and be whole
hook: bend and be straight, empty and be full (Tao Te Ching 22)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter twenty-one: the Way, dim and slippery, and yet with something real inside it. Your line was something real. What did you name as real that you couldn't measure? Day one thousand eighty-four.

A couch is stuck in a doorway. One person is on the hall side, shoving. The other is inside the room, pulling. The couch doesn't move, and both of them are getting louder. Then a neighbor wanders past, looks for a second, and says, tilt it. Stand it on its end, turn it a little. The couch slides through as if the doorway had grown. Nobody got stronger. Somebody gave up the straight line. Chapter twenty-two of the Tao Te Ching is built on that moment, when bending is what gets the thing through.
screen: `A COUCH IN A DOORWAY.` → `SHOVE, PULL, NOTHING.` → `TILT IT.`

segments.voice: First, bent, then whole. The chapter opens with a run of reversals. In Legge's translation: "The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new." Each pair goes against common sense. We expect the straight to stay straight and the bent to break. The chapter says the bent thing is the one that stays whole. Second, empty, then full. A cup that's already full can't receive; only an empty one can be filled. What is worn out makes room for what is new. The chapter folds wanting into the same pattern: whoever wants little, it says, gets it, and whoever wants a lot gets lost. Third, the sage doesn't push. Then the chapter turns to a person. The sage, it says, doesn't put himself on display, and so he shines. He doesn't insist he's right, and so he stands out. He doesn't boast, and so his work counts. He isn't proud of himself, and so he lasts. Fourth, no one can contend. Here's the part that sounds almost like strategy. Because the sage doesn't contend with anyone, the chapter says, no one in the world can contend with him. There's nothing to push against. And the chapter closes by asking whether the old saying about the bent being made whole was just empty words. Its answer: no. Becoming whole, it says, really comes this way. Yielding here isn't losing. It's how the couch gets through the door.
screen: `BENT, THEN WHOLE.` · `EMPTY, THEN FULL.` · `THE SAGE DOESN'T PUSH.` · `NO ONE CAN CONTEND.` · then, large: `THE CROOKED, STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one small point to yield on. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a small standoff in your life right now: where the dishes go, which route to take, the right way to load something, a comment you've been waiting to correct. Keep it small. Now picture yourself letting it go, saying fine, your way, and meaning it. Notice what happens in your shoulders when you picture that. If it feels like losing, stay with it a moment longer. The bell holds the time.
Yield and be whole. Chapter twenty-two's run of reversals: the bent made whole, the empty filled, and the one who doesn't contend, whom no one can contend with. Today's word.
Your line: yield and be whole. Give way on that one small point today, out loud, without a sigh, and watch what moves. Day one thousand eighty-four.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter twenty-two as a habit for daily life: giving way on small disagreements rather than pressing to win them.

original.note: Chinese, qū zé quán: bent, then whole. The opening words of Tao Te Ching 22.

trapdoor: what you thought: yield and be whole means always give in.
what it means: bending gets things through; the empty can be filled; the one who doesn't contend has nothing to push against.
what a scholar hears: qu ze quan, the bent is whole, an old saying the chapter quotes and then insists is not empty words.

notes: Verify the Legge 1891 wording: 'The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new.'

The rest of chapter 22 is paraphrased: few and many desires; the four 'doesn't ... and so ...' lines about the sage; 'because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him'; the closing claim that the ancients' saying is not empty words. Confirm.
The outline hook says 'bend and be straight'; the opening Chinese 曲則全 is more literally 'bent, then whole', and the 'crooked, straight' line follows. Both are covered.
The couch scene is an illustration, not a source.
Pronunciation guide for 曲則全 is approximate.
Editor: rewrote the 'worn-out shoe gets replaced' line, which didn't fit the chapter's point that the worn out becomes new; otherwise checked against Legge's chapter 22 and left as is.
